content.text: USER: I'm in need of a 3D video game that I can play online with my friends. Something like an online skate park where we can go and do tricks and stuff

content.thinking: The user wants a 3D video game they can play online with friends, specifically an online skate park where they can do tricks. This is essentially a request for a multiplayer 3D environment with physics for skateboarding. I need to propose a solution that meets the requirements: 3D graphics, online multiplayer, ability to perform tricks. I should choose a web-friendly stack because the user likely wants something they can run in a browser and share with friends easily. Three.js is a solid choice for rendering 3D graphics in the browser. For the multiplayer aspect, a lightweight real-time communication layer is needed; a Node.js server with WebSocket support (e.g., using the ws library or socket.io) can handle synchronizing player positions and actions. I also need to mention that I’ll check the workspace first – this signals that I will inspect any existing project files before starting to generate code, which is a good practice to avoid overwriting or duplicating work. This phrasing also aligns with the pattern of first confirming the environment before proceeding. Therefore, the appropriate response is to tell the user I’ll build a 3D multiplayer skate park using Three.js for graphics and a Node.js WebSocket server for networking, and that I’ll first check the workspace. This directly addresses the request and sets up the next step of inspecting the workspace.

content.text: I'll build you a 3D multiplayer skate park game — Three.js for the graphics, a Node.js WebSocket server so you and your friends can join the same park. Let me check the workspace first.
